claim: Seven adult male mice (1–4 months old) were used in this study.
source: A total of seven adult male mice (1–4 months old) were used in this study.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing the animals used.

claim: The mice used were triple transgenic Rasgrf2-2A-dCre; CamK2a-tTA;TITL-GCaMP6f animals expressing GCaMP6f in excitatory neocortical layer 2/3 neurons.
source: These mice were triple transgenic Rasgrf2-2A-dCre; CamK2a-tTA;TITL-GCaMP6f animals, expressing GCaMP6f in excitatory neocortical layer 2/3 neurons (Gilad and Helmchen, 2020).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section with citation to previous work.

claim: The dataset used in this study is identical to the one published in Gilad and Helmchen, 2020.
source: This dataset is identical to the one published in Gilad and Helmchen, 2020 where we focused only on learning dynamics.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the Results section with citation.

claim: Trial history information in barrel cortex (BC) emerges only as the mouse learned the task.
source: We found trial history information in barrel cortex (BC) during stimulus presentation. Importantly, trial history in BC emerged only as the mouse learned the task.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Trial history information in rostrolateral (RL) association cortex emerges before stimulus presentation.
source: Next, we also found learning-dependent trial history information in rostrolateral (RL) association cortex that emerges before stimulus presentation, preceding activity in BC.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: BC displayed higher activity during CR-Hit compared to Hit-Hit only during learning and expert phases, but not during the naive period.
source: BC displayed higher activity during CR-Hit compared to Hit-Hit only during learning and expert phases, but not during the naive period (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in Results section with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: The difference in BC activity between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit was significant during the stim period in learning and expert phases across mice.
source: This difference was significant during the stim period in learning and expert phases across mice (Figure 2b; two-way analysis of variance [ANOVA] with repeated measures; DF(1-6) F = 51 p < 0.001, DF(2-12) F = 18 p < 0.001, DF(2-12) F = 5 p < 0.05 for trial history, learning, and the interaction between trial history and learning; post hoc Tukey analysis p < 0.05 for trial history in learning and expert phases; p > 0.05 in the naive phase).
evidence: Statistical analysis results are provided with specific test parameters and p-values.

claim: Body movements and whisker envelope were similar between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit pairs.
source: Both body movements and whisker envelope were similar between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit pairs (Figure 2c) and there was no significant difference across mice during the stim period for neither naive, learning, or expert phases (Figure 2d, p > 0.05; signed-rank test) nor during the pre period (p > 0.05, signed-rank test, data not shown).
evidence: Stated with statistical test results and figure references.

claim: Responses during the reward period in cortex and specifically in BC went back to baseline 4–5 s after the start of the reward period.
source: We further report that responses during the reward period in cortex and specifically in BC went back to baseline 4–5 s after the start of the reward period and 6–8 s before the presentation of the next stimulus (total inter-trial interval ranged between 10 and 12 s).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section describing temporal dynamics.

claim: Responses in BC during the reward period were not consistently modulated as a function of learning.
source: In addition, responses in BC during the reward period were not consistently modulated as a function of learning (p > 0.05; Wilcoxon signed-rank test between naive and expert, BC response averaged during the reward period, 2–4 s after stimulus onset; n = 7 mice).
evidence: Statistical test results provided showing no significant modulation.

claim: Direct responses from the reward period do not affect history-related responses during the next trial.
source: Taken together, we find that direct responses from the reward period do not affect history-related responses during the next trial.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the temporal analysis of reward period responses.

claim: The corrected signal (473 signal minus the 405 signal) maintained a significant trial history difference between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit conditions during learning and expert phases, but not during the naive phase.
source: The corrected signal (473 signal minus the 405 signal; see Materials and methods) maintained a significant trial history difference between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit conditions during learning and expert phases, but not during the naive phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Results from hemodynamic correction experiments with figure reference.

claim: Two photon imaging of single cells in BC and RL during the expert phase found significant trial history differences.
source: Finally, we further performed two photon imaging of single cells in BC and RL during the expert phase and found significant trial history differences, that is, higher response in CR-Hit compared to Hit-Hit in BC (during the stim period) and RL (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; during the pre period).
evidence: Results from two-photon imaging experiments with figure reference.

claim: Non-calcium dynamics such as hemodynamics have a minor effect on the results, specifically regarding trial history differences.
source: Taken together, non-calcium dynamics such as hemodynamics have a minor effect the results, specifically regarding trial history differences.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple control experiments.

claim: History modulation in BC had the steepest increase after mice crossed their learning threshold.
source: History modulation in BC had the steepest increase after mice crossed their learning threshold (Figure 3e, f).
evidence: Stated in Results with figure reference showing the data.

claim: The onset of the history modulation was found to occur shortly after the learning threshold, highly correlated with the learning threshold.
source: The onset of the history modulation was defined as the first trial bin exceeding mean ± 2 standard deviation of trial-shuffled sample distribution and was found to occur shortly after the learning threshold, highly correlated with the learning threshold indicating strong relationship between history emergence and learning of each individual mouse (Figure 3g, h; 500 ± 221 trials, median ± SEM, r = 0.97, p < 0.001, Spearman correlation).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis provided with specific values.

claim: Response in BC for FA-Hit was similar to Hit-Hit and significantly lower compared to CR-Hit.
source: Response in BC for FA-Hit was similar to Hit-Hit and significantly lower compared to CR-Hit (Figure 2—figure supplement 7; p < 0.05 signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical comparison results with figure reference.

claim: A preceding CR trial resulted in higher activation independent of the current trial type.
source: In general, a preceding CR trial resulted in higher activation independent of the current trial type (i.e., Hit, CR, or FA; not significant for CR and FA), indicating that history information is present at the current time independently of incoming sensory information (Figure 2—figure supplement 7; compare orange bars to the blue bars).
evidence: Pattern observed across different trial type comparisons with figure reference.

claim: RL activity was significantly higher in CR-Hit compared to Hit-Hit trials in the pre period during the expert phase.
source: RL activity was significantly higher in CR-Hit compared to Hit-Hit trials in the pre period during the expert phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; signed-rank test, p < 0.05, similar trend for the learning phase but insignificant; not significant for the naive phase).
evidence: Statistical test results with figure reference.

claim: The onset of history modulation within the trial structure was earlier in RL compared to BC in both learning and expert phases but not significantly different.
source: The onset of history modulation within the trial structure (as in Figure 3d) was earlier in RL compared to BC in both learning (−0.15 ± 0.85 and 0.05 ± 0.86 s, median ± SD in RL and BC, respectively) and expert phases (−0.75 ± 0.53 and −0.1 ± 0.74 s, median ± SD in RL and BC, respectively) but not significantly different (p > 0.05, signed-rank test).
evidence: Temporal comparison with statistical test results.

claim: During the expert phase, history AUC in both BC and RL has a discrimination power in the stim period that is not significantly different than that of the current AUC.
source: Interestingly, during the expert phase, history AUC in both BC and RL has a discrimination power in the stim period that is not significantly different than that of the current AUC (Figure 6b, c; p > 0.05; singed rank test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of AUC values with figure reference.

claim: BC and RL discriminate past stimuli just as well as the current stimuli.
source: In other words, we found that BC and RL discriminate past stimuli just as well as the current stimuli.
evidence: Interpretation of the AUC comparison results.

claim: During the learning phase, RL and to some extent BC, display a significantly higher history AUC compared to the current AUC, specifically in the pre period.
source: In addition, during the learning phase, RL and to some extent BC, display a significantly higher history AUC compared to the current AUC, specifically in the pre period (Figure 6d, e; p < 0.05; singed rank test).
evidence: Statistical comparison with figure reference.

claim: History information is discriminative at the single trial level before stimulus onset.
source: This indicates that history information is discriminative at the single trial level before stimulus onset.
evidence: Interpretation of the pre-period AUC results.

claim: RL displays the highest history AUC during the pre period, whereas BC displays the highest history AUC values during the stim period.
source: Quantified across 25 areas and averaged across mice, RL displays the highest history AUC during the pre period, whereas BC displays the highest history AUC values during the stim period (Figure 6h, i).
evidence: Quantitative comparison across cortical areas with figure reference.

claim: Trial history emerges in RL before the texture arrives and then shifts to BC during stimulus presentation.
source: In summary, we find that trial history emerges in RL before the texture arrives and then shifts to BC during stimulus presentation.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the temporal and spatial analysis of trial history.

claim: Trial history encoding was not dependent on the current stimulus.
source: Trial history encoding was not dependent on the current stimulus and emerged at RL association area before texture touch.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a main finding.

claim: A previous CR trial will lead to higher activity in BC and RL compared to a previous Hit trial.
source: Our results indicate that a previous CR trial will lead to higher activity in BC and RL compared to a previous Hit trial.
evidence: Summary of the main finding in the Discussion.

claim: The difference in activity between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit is probably not due to pure sensory differences in the previous trial since the effect was not present after FA trials.
source: This difference is probably not due to pure sensory differences in the previous trial since the effect was not present after FA trials (sup Figure 2—figure supplement 7, left panel).
evidence: Inference based on comparison with FA trials with figure reference.

claim: The fact that these differences emerged only after learning implies that these differences are not purely sensory or motor related but rather reflect internal history-related information.
source: The fact that these differences emerged only after learning implies that these differences are not purely sensory or motor related but rather reflect internal history-related information.
evidence: Interpretation of the learning-dependent emergence of trial history.

claim: BC carries trial history information during the sensation period which is related to the previous trial several seconds back.
source: We additionally found that BC carries trial history information during the sensation period which is related to the previous trial several seconds back.
evidence: Summary statement in the Discussion.

claim: Trial history information emerges in RL before texture touch, implying that RL may transfer past experience in a top-down manner to BC for optimal sensory integration.
source: Interestingly, we show that trial history information emerges in RL before texture touch, implying that RL may transfer past experience in a top-down manner to BC for optimal sensory integration.
evidence: Interpretation of the temporal relationship between RL and BC activity.

claim: RL is the lateral part of the PPC adjacent to BC, within the cluster of higher-order association areas surrounding V1.
source: RL is the lateral part of the PPC adjacent to BC, within the cluster of higher-order association areas surrounding V1 (Hovde et al., 2019; Lyamzin and Benucci, 2019).
evidence: Anatomical description with citations.

claim: Previous studies showed that trial history of choice outcome is encoded by PPC neurons.
source: Previous studies showed that trial history of choice outcome is encoded by PPC neurons (Harvey et al., 2012; Hwang et al., 2017; Morcos and Harvey, 2016; Pho et al., 2018), as well as history of sensory information (Akrami et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of previous literature with citations.

claim: Silencing the PPC specifically during the inter-trial interval affected the behavioral performance of rats.
source: Silencing the PPC specifically during the inter-trial interval affected the behavioral performance of rats (Akrami et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017), whereas silencing during the stimulus presentation did not affected performance.
evidence: Summary of previous experimental findings with citations.

claim: The PPC is reciprocally connected to hippocampus via entorhinal and retrosplenial cortices.
source: The PPC is also reciprocally connected to hippocampus via entorhinal and retrosplenial cortices (Save and Poucet, 2009; Whitlock et al., 2008) and to basolateral amygdala via the anterior cingulate cortex (Suzuki et al., 2022), giving fast access to the different memory hubs.
evidence: Anatomical connectivity information with citations.

claim: Khodagholy et al. showed coupling of PPC and hippocampal ripples that strengthen in non-REM sleep after rats learned a spatial exploration task.
source: (Khodagholy et al., 2017) showed coupling of PPC and hippocampal ripples that strengthen in non-REM (Rapid eye movement) sleep after rats learned a spatial exploration task, further indicating that RL may relay history information from subcortical memory hubs to cortex.
evidence: Summary of previous findings with citation and interpretation.

claim: The fact that trial history emerges only after learning implies that it encodes a subjective value or association of a certain past stimulus.
source: The fact that trial history emerges only after learning, implies that it encodes a subjective value or association of a certain past stimulus.
evidence: Interpretation of the learning-dependent emergence.

claim: The consolidation of a certain association induces long-term synaptic plasticity of top-down projections from higher-order association area to a lower-order sensory area.
source: In light of this discussion, we suggest that the consolidation of a certain association (in our case a CR), induces long-term synaptic plasticity of top-down projections from higher-order association area (e.g., RL) to a lower-order sensory area (e.g., BC).
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on the findings.

claim: This projection-specific potentiation may facilitate the recruitment sensory cortex in the context of the immediate previous history.
source: This projection-specific potentiation may facilitate the recruitment sensory cortex in the context of the immediate previous history.
evidence: Proposed functional consequence of the mechanism.

claim: The wide-field signal measured in this study reports bulk population activity specifically in L2/3 excitatory cells.
source: The wide-field signal measured in our study reports bulk population activity specifically in L2/3 excitatory cells.
evidence: Description of the measurement method.

claim: Previous studies that measured single cell activity in the BC showed that single cells tend to respond to one information type.
source: On the other side, previous studies that measured single cell activity in the BC showed that single cells tend to respond to one information type (Chéreau et al., 2020; Estebanez et al., 2012; Rodgers et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of previous findings with citations.

claim: Different populations in BC encode current and history information, which leads to a larger fraction of neurons in BC that are active for the CR-Hit pair.
source: In this case, we hypothesize that different populations in BC encode current and history information, which leads to a larger fraction of neurons in BC that are active for the CR-Hit pair.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed based on previous findings.

claim: A larger number of active neurons in BC may facilitate sensorimotor integration involving downstream areas such as the motor cortex, further resulting in gaining expertise.
source: A larger number of active neurons in BC may facilitate sensorimotor integration involving downstream areas such as the motor cortex, further resulting in gaining expertise (Zuo and Diamond, 2019).
evidence: Proposed mechanism with citation.

claim: Both history and learning involve other circuit elements such as deep cortical layers, inhibitory subtypes, other pathways, and subcortical areas.
source: It is probable that both history and learning involve other circuit elements such as deep cortical layers (Pasupathy and Miller, 2005; Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018; Vecchia et al., 2020), inhibitory subtypes, other pathways (Lacefield et al., 2019; Mohan et al., 2022; Musall et al., 2023; Petreanu et al., 2012; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019), and subcortical areas (Fu et al., 2015; Garrett et al., 2020; Pasupathy and Miller, 2005; Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: Discussion of broader circuit involvement with citations.

claim: As we learn, the cortex learns to better integrate past and present information resulting in expert performance.
source: In summary, our results imply that as we learn, the cortex learns to better integrate past and present information resulting in expert performance.
evidence: Summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Five mice were trained to lick for the P100 texture and two mice were trained to lick for the P1200 texture.
source: Five mice were trained to lick for the P100 and two mice were trained to lick for the P1200 texture.
evidence: Experimental design details stated in Results.

claim: Mice were rewarded in 'Hit' trials for correctly licking after the go texture and punished with white noise for incorrectly licking for the no-go texture.
source: Mice were rewarded in 'Hit' trials for correctly licking after the go texture and punished with white noise for incorrectly licking for the no-go texture ('false alarm' trials, FA).
evidence: Task structure description.

claim: The performance of all mice increased with training and eventually reached high discrimination levels.
source: The performance of all mice increased with training (5–11 days; ~500 trials/day) and eventually reached high discrimination levels (quantified by d′; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Gilad et al., 2018; Materials and methods).
evidence: Behavioral results with figure reference.

claim: Six out of the seven mice learned the task within 3–4 days after around a thousand trials.
source: Six out of the seven mice learned the task within 3–4 days after around a thousand trials (Supplementary Fig. 1).
evidence: Learning timeline data with figure reference.

claim: Mouse #4 learned the task within 10 days.
source: Mouse #4 learned the task within 10 days.
evidence: Individual mouse learning data.

claim: All mice, after gaining expertise, showed strong activation in the BC during stimulus representation, stronger in Hit trials compared to CR trials.
source: All mice, after gaining expertise, showed strong activation in the BC (Figure 1d, upper panel). This activation was during stimulus representation, stronger in Hit trials compared to CR trials (Figure 1d, lower panel), not dependent on the texture type (i.e., if the hit was P100 or P1200).
evidence: Imaging results with figure reference.

claim: Learning curves that are calculated separately for each pair (i.e., either a preceding Hit or CR trial) were not significantly different.
source: We note that learning curves that are calculated separately for each pair (i.e., either a preceding Hit or CR trial) were not significantly different (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical comparison with figure reference.

claim: FA probabilities did not significantly differ based on the preceding trial type.
source: We further note FA probabilities did not significantly differ based on the preceding trial type (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis with figure reference.

claim: The lick reaction time (but not the lick rate) between Hit-Hit and CR-Hit were significantly different.
source: In addition, the lick reaction time (but not the lick rate) between Hit-Hit and CR-Hit were significantly different (p < 0.05; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Statistical test results.

claim: The first touch occurred on average 0.33 and 0.34 s before the texture stopped for naive and expert mice, respectively.
source: The first touch occurred on average 0.33 and 0.34 s before the texture stopped for naive and expert mice, respectively.
evidence: Timing measurement from whisker tracking.

claim: Time of first touch did not differ between expert and naive mice.
source: Time of first touch did not differ between expert and naive mice (p > 0.05; Mann–Whitney U-test; n = 7 mice).
evidence: Statistical comparison result.

claim: The first touch occurred mostly (but not exclusively) in the pre period from −1 to −0.5 relative to texture stop.
source: We note that the first touch occurred mostly (but not exclusively) in the pre period from −1 to −0.5 relative to texture stop.
evidence: Temporal analysis of whisker-texture contact.

claim: A statistical comparison between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit responses within each mouse separately maintained significance for expert (7/7 mice) and learning (6/7 mice) but not for naive (0/7 mice).
source: In addition, a statistical comparison between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit responses within each mouse separately maintained significance for expert (7/7 mice; Mann–Whitney U-test p < 0.05) and learning (6/7 mice) but not for naive (0/7 mice) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Within-mouse statistical analysis with figure reference.

claim: A statistical comparison between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit responses in RL within each mouse separately maintained significance for expert phase (5/7 mice).
source: In addition, a statistical comparison between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit responses in RL within each mouse separately maintained significance for expert phase (5/7 mice; Mann–Whitney U-test p < 0.05).
evidence: Within-mouse statistical analysis for RL.

claim: Body movements and whisker parameters did not significantly differ between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit conditions during the pre period.
source: Body movements and whisker parameters did not significantly differ between CR-Hit and Hit-Hit conditions during the pre period (Similar to the stim period. Across and within mice. p > 0.05; Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of movement parameters.

claim: A within mouse statistical comparison between body or whisker parameters in CR-Hit and Hit-Hit maintained a non-significant difference in expert (1/7 mice were significantly different), learning (2/7 mice) and naive (0/7 mice).
source: A within mouse statistical comparison between body or whisker parameters in CR-Hit and Hit-Hit maintained a non-significant difference in expert (1/7 mice were significantly different; Mann–Whitney U-test p > 0.05), learning (2/7 mice) and naive (0/7 mice).
evidence: Within-mouse movement analysis.

claim: Additional cortical areas such as other association areas also display high history AUC values.
source: We note that additional cortical areas such as other association areas also display high history AUC values.
evidence: Observation from AUC analysis across cortical areas.

claim: The onset for the history modulation with relation to the learning profile in RL was earlier than BC, but not significantly different.
source: The onset for the history modulation with relation to the learning profile in RL (similar to Figure 3h; During the pre period) was also earlier than BC, but not significantly different (200 ± 431 trials after crossing threshold compared to 500 ± 221 in BC; median ± SD, p > 0.05 singed rank test).
evidence: Temporal comparison with statistical test.
